# Is a Home Battery Worthwhile Without Solar Panels? A Financial Assessment for an English Household (July 2026)

---

## 1. Scope and Assumptions

**Household profile:** ~9,000 kWh/year electricity consumption; flat rate ~£0.247/kWh; gas heating; SMETS2 smart meter; home office using 10–20 kWh/day predominantly during daytime working hours; limited ability to shift consumption manually; property owner expecting to remain ≥10 years; primary goal is financial saving; no solar panels planned.

**Key technical assumptions:**

| Parameter | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Usable capacity, 5 kWh battery | ~4.8 kWh (95% DoD) | [S20] |
| Usable capacity, 10 kWh battery | ~9.6 kWh (95% DoD) | [S20] |
| Round-trip efficiency (AC-coupled) | ~90% (LFP best-in-class; residential range 85–90%) | [S23][S26] |
| Effective stored kWh delivered, 5 kWh | ~4.3 kWh/cycle | Derived |
| Effective stored kWh delivered, 10 kWh | ~8.6 kWh/cycle | Derived |
| Battery lifespan | 10–12 years; ~6,000–10,000 cycles | [S6][S20][S23] |
| Annual degradation | ~2%/year capacity loss (manufacturer-guaranteed ceiling) | [S26] |
| Maintenance cost | <£100/year | [S3] |
| VAT on installation | 0% until March 2027, then 5% | [S6][S9] |

**On cycling frequency:** Fewer than one full cycle per day is realistic even for optimised systems [S26]. This household's 10–20 kWh/day daytime demand is sufficient to absorb full battery discharge, supporting daily cycling — but only if the battery management system is correctly programmed and the overnight window reliably fills the battery. 330 cycles/year is adopted (allowing ~35 days for partial cycles, grid issues, or tariff changes).

---

## 2. Installed Costs

| System | Low estimate | Mid estimate | High estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~5 kWh installed | £2,800 [S20] | £3,500–£4,200 [S3][S6] | £4,600 [S20] |
| ~10 kWh installed | £5,350 [S20] | £5,500–£6,850 [S20] | £8,000–£9,500 [S8][S9] |

**Adopted central estimates:** £4,000 for a 5 kWh system; £6,500 for a 10 kWh system. The AlphaESS G3 (10 kWh) at £5,350–£6,850 installed [S20] and the Tesla Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh) at £7,750–£8,750 [S20] bracket the 10 kWh range. One source cites a ~16 kWh system installed for ~£3,300 via a DIY-assisted route [S25], and a Reddit report of ~£3,800 for a 16.1 kWh Fogstar system [S21]; both are unverified outliers excluded from the central model but noted as evidence that aggressive pricing exists.

**VAT note:** 0% VAT applies until March 2027 [S6][S9], adding ~£200–£325 if delayed.

---

## 3. Tariff Landscape (July 2026)

### 3.1 Flat-rate baseline
The Ofgem price cap from 1 July 2026 sets the standard variable rate at **26.11p/kWh** with a 57.19p/day standing charge [S14][S17][S18]. The household's ~24.7p/kWh is consistent with a competitive fixed tariff [S13][S17]. Forecasts point to further rises toward October 2026 [S18].

**Annual unit cost at 9,000 kWh:** ~£2,223 (plus ~£209 standing charges = ~£2,432 total).

### 3.2 Time-of-use tariff rates (July 2026)

| Tariff | Off-peak rate | Off-peak window | Peak/day rate | Eligibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Octopus Go | ~7p/kWh | 00:30–05:30 (5 hrs) | ~26.11p | Smart meter; no EV required [S16] |
| Intelligent Octopus Go | ~5.5–8p/kWh | 23:30–05:30 (6 hrs) | ~26.11p | Requires compatible EV or charger [S19] |
| Economy 7 | ~8–10p/kWh | ~7 hrs overnight | ~20–24p daytime | Smart or legacy meter |

**Central case:** 7p off-peak, 26.11p peak (Octopus Go) [S14][S16][S17]. Intelligent Go is excluded as the household has no EV [S19].

**Gross arbitrage spread:** 26.11p − 7p = **19.1p/kWh**

**Net saving per kWh displaced by battery:**
26.11p − (7p ÷ 0.90) = 26.11p − 7.78p = **~18.3p/kWh**

---

## 4. Option 2: TOU Tariff Without a Battery

The home office consumes 10–20 kWh/day during daytime hours — consumption that cannot be shifted to the overnight window without a battery. On Octopus Go, the day rate (~26.11p) exceeds the household's flat rate (~24.7p) by ~1.4p/kWh.

**Estimate at 9,000 kWh/year:**
- 20% of consumption (1,800 kWh) shifted to off-peak: saves (24.7p − 7p) × 1,800 = **£319/year**
- 80% (7,200 kWh) at 26.11p vs 24.7p: costs an extra 1.41p × 7,200 = **£102/year**
- **Net saving: approximately £217/year**

If only 10% is shifted, the net saving falls to ~£100/year; if none is shifted, the household pays slightly more. The saving is real but fragile and depends entirely on genuine overnight load-shifting.

---

## 5. Battery Scenarios: Financial Modelling

### 5.1 Annual savings (Year 1, before degradation)

Net saving per kWh displaced: **18.3p** (central case). Assume 70% of discharged energy usefully displaces peak-rate consumption (accounting for loads that cannot be timed to battery discharge):

| Scenario | Delivered kWh/cycle | Useful displacement (70%) | Saving/kWh | Cycles/yr | **Annual saving** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 kWh + Go | 4.3 kWh | 3.0 kWh | 18.3p | 330 | **~£181** |
| 10 kWh + Go | 8.6 kWh | 6.0 kWh | 18.3p | 330 | **~£362** |

**Contrast with marketing claims:** One installer source claims £800–£950/year from Octopus Go arbitrage alone, plus £120–£300/year from VPP participation [S22]. These figures are not reconcilable with the arithmetic above at 7p/26.11p rates and 9,000 kWh/year consumption, and should be treated as upper-bound marketing estimates. They may assume larger batteries, higher peak rates, or near-100% displacement efficiency. The VPP income figure (£120–£300/year) is noted separately below.

### 5.2 Virtual Power Plant (VPP) income
Battery owners can enrol in VPP schemes via platforms such as Axle Energy or through Octopus/Tesla programmes, earning payments for grid services during demand peaks [S22]. Reported income is £120–£300/year [S22]. This income is tax-free under HMRC's £1,000 trading allowance for most households, and VPP cycling is described as minimal relative to LFP warranty limits [S22]. However, this source is commercially motivated (battery installer) and the figures are unverified by independent sources. VPP income is therefore treated as an **upside scenario only**, not included in the central model.

**If VPP income of £150/year (conservative mid-point) is included:**
- 5 kWh annual saving: £181 + £150 = ~£331/year
- 10 kWh annual saving: £362 + £150 = ~£512/year

### 5.3 Degradation over 10 years
At ~2%/year [S26], average usable capacity over 10 years is ~90% of Year 1. Effective multiplier: ~9.5 years equivalent.

**Central model (no VPP):**
- 5 kWh: cumulative 10-year saving ≈ £181 × 9.5 = **~£1,720**
- 10 kWh: cumulative 10-year saving ≈ £362 × 9.5 = **~£3,439**

**With VPP (upside scenario):**
- 5 kWh: ~£331 × 9.5 = **~£3,145**
- 10 kWh: ~£512 × 9.5 = **~£4,864**

### 5.4 Costs over 10 years

| Item | 5 kWh | 10 kWh |
|---|---|---|
| Installation (central) | £4,000 | £6,500 |
| Maintenance (10 yr) | £500 | £500 |
| Inverter replacement risk | £0–£1,000 | £0–£1,000 |
| **Total cost (central)** | **£4,500** | **£7,000** |

Battery replacement within 10 years is unlikely given 6,000–10,000 cycle ratings and 10–15 year warranties [S6][S20][S23]. Inverter failure remains a real risk.

### 5.5 10-year net financial outcome

| Option | 10-yr saving | 10-yr cost | **Net 10-yr outcome** | Simple payback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flat rate, no battery | £0 | £0 | Baseline | — |
| TOU tariff, no battery | ~£1,000–£2,000 | £0 | **+£1,000–£2,000** | Immediate |
| 5 kWh + Go (central) | £1,720 | £4,500 | **−£2,780** | ~25 years |
| 10 kWh + Go (central) | £3,439 | £7,000 | **−£3,561** | ~19 years |
| 10 kWh + Go + VPP (upside) | £4,864 | £7,000 | **−£2,136** | ~14 years |

Even the VPP upside scenario does not produce 10-year payback at central costs.

---

## 6. Sensitivity Analysis

### 6.1 Annual consumption

| Consumption | TOU no battery (net 10yr) | 5 kWh net (10yr) | 10 kWh net (10yr) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6,000 kWh/yr | +£650–£1,300 | ~−£2,900 | ~−£3,700 |
| 9,000 kWh/yr | +£1,000–£2,000 | ~−£2,780 | ~−£3,561 |
| 11,000 kWh/yr | +£1,200–£2,400 | ~−£2,650 | ~−£3,350 |

Higher consumption improves TOU-without-battery outcomes but only marginally improves battery outcomes since battery capacity is fixed.

### 6.2 Tariff spread sensitivity (10 kWh battery)

| Off-peak | Peak | Net saving/kWh | Annual saving | 10-yr net outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.5p (Intelligent Go) | 26.11p | 20.0p | ~£396 | ~−£3,240 |
| 7p (Go, central) | 26.11p | 18.3p | ~£362 | ~−£3,561 |
| 7p | 30p (future rise) | 22.2p | ~£440 | ~−£2,820 |
| 10p (Economy 7) | 24.7p | 13.6p | ~£270 | ~−£4,435 |
| 14.75p (Economy 7 high) | 35.17p [S25] | 18.5p | ~£366 | ~−£3,530 |

No realistic spread produces 10-year payback at central costs. The Economy 7 scenario at 14.75p/35.17p [S25] — which one source uses to claim a 3.4-year payback — relies on a £3,300 installed cost for a 16 kWh system via a DIY-assisted route, not a professionally installed 10 kWh system at £6,500. That scenario is not applicable here.

### 6.3 Installation cost sensitivity (10 kWh battery)

| Install cost | 10-yr saving | **Net 10-yr outcome** | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|
| £5,350 (AlphaESS G3 low) [S20] | £3,439 | **−£2,411** | ~16 years |
| £6,500 (central) | £3,439 | **−£3,561** | ~19 years |
| £6,850 (AlphaESS G3 high) [S20] | £3,439 | **−£3,911** | ~20 years |
| £8,750 (Powerwall 3) [S20] | £3,439 | **−£5,811** | ~26 years |

### 6.4 Peak consumption proportion sensitivity
If the household shifts 40% of consumption overnight (rather than 20%):
- TOU without battery: ~£400–£500/year, ~£4,000–£5,000 over 10 years — a strong positive outcome at zero capital cost
- Battery savings increase by ~10–15% — insufficient to change the fundamental conclusion

### 6.5 Degradation sensitivity
At 1%/year (optimistic): 10-year saving increases ~5%. At 3%/year: decreases ~5%. Not material to the conclusion [S26].

### 6.6 Electricity price trajectory
Forecasts suggest the price cap may rise toward October 2026 [S18]. A sustained peak rate of 30p+ would improve battery economics but still falls short of 10-year payback at central costs. Rising prices also increase the value of the TOU-without-battery option proportionally.

---

## 7. Additional Risk Factors

**Tariff uncertainty:** Octopus Go rates are not Ofgem-regulated and can change. The quarterly price cap review cycle introduces ongoing volatility [S14][S17].

**Manufacturer stability:** GivEnergy entered administration in 2026 [S10], illustrating that warranty and software support continuity is a genuine risk. AlphaESS and Tesla Powerwall have stronger market positions [S20] but no manufacturer is risk-free. Confirm what recourse exists if a manufacturer ceases trading before purchasing.

**Inverter replacement:** Hybrid inverters may require replacement within 10–15 years, adding £500–£1,500 to costs not fully captured in the central model.

**Intelligent Go ineligibility:** The cheapest off-peak rates (~5.5–8p) on Intelligent Go require a compatible EV or charger [S19]. Without an EV, the household is limited to standard Octopus Go (~7p).

**VPP income uncertainty:** The £120–£300/year VPP figure [S22] comes from a battery installer and is unverified independently. VPP scheme availability, payment rates, and eligibility criteria may change.

**DIY/low-cost routes:** Installed costs of £3,300–£3,800 for larger systems appear achievable via DIY-assisted or competitive-tender routes [S21][S25], but exclude professional commissioning, grid registration, and warranty protection. These routes carry higher risk and are not recommended without specialist knowledge.

---

## 8. Conclusions

### Does either battery pay for itself within 10 years?
**No — under central assumptions.** At central installed costs, neither a 5 kWh (~25-year payback) nor a 10 kWh (~19-year payback) battery pays back within 10 years through tariff arbitrage alone. Even at the lowest credible professionally installed cost for a 10 kWh system (£5,350 [S20]), payback extends to ~16 years. Including VPP income at an optimistic £150/year shortens payback to ~14 years for a 10 kWh system — still outside the 10-year horizon.

The 3.4-year payback claimed by one source [S25] relies on a £3,300 DIY-assisted installation of a 16 kWh system on a high-spread Economy 7 tariff (14.75p/35.17p). That scenario does not apply to a professionally installed 10 kWh system at market rates on Octopus Go.

### Does switching tariff without a battery provide meaningful savings?
**Yes — modestly, and only with genuine load-shifting.** If the household can shift 15–20% of consumption to the overnight window (dishwasher, washing machine, overnight device charging), Octopus Go saves approximately £100–£320/year at zero capital cost — a positive 10-year outcome of £1,000–£3,000. This is the most financially efficient action available.

### Conditions under which the conclusion changes
- Installation cost falls to ~£3,500–£4,000 for a 10 kWh system (possible with competitive quotes or future price falls)
- The tariff spread widens significantly and durably (e.g., off-peak 5.5p, peak 35p+)
- The household acquires an EV, unlocking Intelligent Go rates and dramatically increasing cheap overnight consumption
- VPP income proves reliable and sustained at £200+/year
- Solar panels are installed (fundamentally changes the economics — outside scope)
- Electricity prices rise substantially and persistently above current cap levels

### Best financial option
**Switch to a TOU tariff (Octopus Go) without a battery, and maximise overnight load-shifting.** This costs nothing, requires only a tariff switch (the household already has a smart meter), and delivers £100–£320/year in savings. Over 10 years, this outperforms every battery scenario in net financial terms.

**Second-best:** Remain on the current competitive flat-rate tariff if overnight load-shifting proves impractical. This avoids capital outlay and any risk of higher bills.

### Strongest argument against this recommendation
The strongest counter-argument is **optionality and future-proofing**: battery costs are falling, tariff spreads may widen, and a battery installed now at 0% VAT (before March 2027 [S6][S9]) positions the household to benefit from future solar installation, vehicle-to-grid tariffs, or VPP grid services. If an installer quote comes in at £4,000–£4,500 for a 10 kWh system — possible given the AlphaESS G3 range [S20] — and VPP income proves reliable at £150+/year, the financial case approaches breakeven over 15 years under favourable tariff conditions. The backup power benefit has real non-financial value that this analysis does not capture.

### What to obtain before any purchase

1. **Half-hourly smart meter data:** Download via Octopus, n3rgy, or the DCC to establish exactly how much consumption falls in the 00:30–05:30 window versus daytime peak hours. This is the single most important input for validating the model.
2. **Tariff modelling first:** Use Octopus Energy's own switching tool to model actual bill impact of Octopus Go against your specific half-hourly profile *before* considering a battery. If the tariff switch alone saves £200+/year, it is the priority action.
3. **At least three installer quotes** for both 5 kWh and 10 kWh systems, specifying LFP chemistry, AC-coupled configuration, full installed cost including inverter, commissioning, and grid registration.
4. **Warranty and manufacturer viability:** Confirm warranty terms and recourse if the manufacturer ceases trading [S10]. Prefer manufacturers with established UK service networks.
5. **Battery management system capability:** Confirm the system can be programmed to charge only during the off-peak window and discharge automatically to meet daytime load without manual intervention — essential for achieving the modelled savings.
6. **VPP scheme terms:** If a battery is purchased, obtain specific terms from Axle Energy or the relevant platform [S22] — payment rates, minimum battery size, cycling obligations, and contract duration — before treating VPP income as a financial input.
7. **EV plans:** If an EV purchase is likely within 2–3 years, Intelligent Octopus Go becomes accessible, improving battery economics materially and potentially changing the recommendation.

findings.title: Battery Storage Cost UK 2026 | Is £2,500–£8,000 Worth It?
findings.rational: This webpage provides UK-specific installed battery storage costs by capacity, standalone (no solar) pricing, brand warranties, payback estimates for tariff arbitrage without solar, and notes on time-of-use tariff compatibility — all directly relevant to assessing whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery is financially worthwhile for a UK household without solar panels.
findings.evidence:
Battery Without Solar (Standalone): 'Batteries can operate without solar panels, charging from cheap overnight grid electricity.' Configuration / Price / Use Case: '5kWh standalone: £4,500–£5,500 — Tariff arbitrage, backup power'; '9.5kWh standalone: £6,500–£8,000 — Higher capacity arbitrage.' 'Standalone batteries make financial sense with time-of-use tariffs like Octopus Go or Intelligent, charging at 7–10p/kWh overnight and avoiding 24–34p/kWh peak rates.'

Payback Scenarios (5kWh at £4,000): 'Tariff arbitrage (no solar): Annual Benefit £250–£400 / Payback 10–16 years.' By contrast, 'Solar + time-of-use tariff: Annual Benefit £400–£550 / Payback 7–10 years.'

Installed price ranges by capacity: '5kWh: £3,500–£4,500 (standalone adds £300–£800 for separate inverter, so effectively £4,500–£5,500 standalone)'; '9.5kWh: £5,500–£7,000 installed with solar context, £6,500–£8,000 standalone.' Cost per kWh stored: '5kWh ~£800/kWh; 9.5kWh ~£658/kWh — larger batteries offer better value per kWh stored.'

Brand/warranty data: Mid-range brands (GivEnergy, Pylontech) carry 10-year warranties; budget brands 5–7 years. GivEnergy 5.2kWh installed: £3,800–£4,300; GivEnergy 9.5kWh installed: £5,800–£6,500 (these are with-solar context prices; standalone premiums apply).

Weaker case indicators listed by the page include: 'Home all day using electricity as solar generates' (analogous to high daytime demand from home office); 'Very low electricity consumption'; 'Tight budget without solar plans'; 'Property unsuitable for solar.' The strong-case indicators all reference solar panels or evening-heavy usage patterns.

Future incentives noted: 'The Warm Homes Plan includes battery storage for low-income households. A £2,500 heat battery grant launches in 2026/27. Future Consumer Loan Scheme (April 2027) will offer government-backed financing.' No current VAT relief or grant specifically for standalone battery-only installs is mentioned.
findings.summary: For a UK household without solar panels, this source indicates standalone 5 kWh battery installation costs £4,500–£5,500 and a ~10 kWh (9.5 kWh) system costs £6,500–£8,000. The site's own payback table for tariff arbitrage without solar shows only £250–£400 annual benefit and a 10–16 year payback on a 5 kWh battery — the longest payback of all scenarios listed. The page explicitly flags high daytime electricity use and no solar plans as factors weakening the financial case. Time-of-use tariffs (Octopus Go/Intelligent) at 7–10p/kWh overnight versus 24–34p/kWh peak are cited as the mechanism for savings. Warranties are 10 years for mid-range brands. No current grants for standalone battery-only installs are identified, though future schemes (2026/27 onwards) are noted. This source is an installer's marketing site and should be treated cautiously; its payback figures likely represent optimistic scenarios and do not account for round-trip losses, degradation, or the household's specific daytime-heavy demand profile.

This directly informs the capital cost assumptions needed to calculate payback periods and 10-year net financial outcomes for the 5 kWh and 10 kWh battery options in the research goal.

Tier 2 (UK Favourites): 'Estimated Retrofit Cost: £4,500 – £6,000 (Installed)' for ~10kWh systems. Specific entries: 'Sunsynk: £4,500 – £5,500 (10kWh) retrofit'; 'Fox ESS: £4,200 – £5,200 (Cube) retrofit'; 'myenergi: £5,800 – £6,900 (10kWh) retrofit.' Package pricing: 'The Saver (3–5kWh, Pylontech/Growatt): £2,500 – £3,500'; 'The UK Standard (9.5–10kWh, Sunsynk): £4,500 – £5,500.' VAT rule: '0% VAT on Battery Storage applies to standalone battery retrofits until 2027. On a £5,000 system, this saves you £1,000 instantly.' Hidden costs noted: AC battery inverter for retrofits without existing compatible hybrid inverter adds '+£800 – £1,200'; backup power (EPS) switchgear adds '+£300 – £600'; DNO fees for systems >3.68kW adds '+£150 – £500.' Cost breakdown for a £5,000 retrofit: hardware ~65% (£3,250), labour ~20% (£1,000), materials/certification ~15% (£750). Note: 'GivEnergy Ltd entered administration in April 2026. findings.summary: For a standalone battery retrofit in England (no existing solar), a ~5 kWh system (Pylontech/Growatt) costs approximately £2,500–£3,500 fully installed at 0% VAT, while a ~10 kWh system (Sunsynk, Fox ESS) costs approximately £4,200–£5,500. These are the key capital cost inputs for payback and 10-year net outcome calculations. The 0% VAT treatment on standalone retrofits (confirmed until at least 2027) is a meaningful saving versus the pre-2022 position. Additional costs for EPS backup switchgear (£300–£600) and DNO notification for larger systems (£150–£500) should be budgeted. GivEnergy should be excluded from consideration due to administration. These figures should be treated as installer-marketing estimates and verified with at least three MCS-certified installer quotes.

findings.summary: For a UK household considering a standalone home battery (no solar) in 2026, this installer source provides useful indicative installed cost benchmarks: roughly £3,200–£4,200 for a 5kWh system and £4,600–£7,100 for a 10kWh system, with LFP chemistry (the recommended type) at the higher end of those ranges. The source should be used only for cost-of-hardware benchmarking, not for savings or payback calculations in a battery-only context. Independent, tariff-specific modelling is required for the financial assessment.

findings.evidence: From the webpage: 'You can install a home battery: alongside a new solar panel system / as a retrofit battery for existing solar panels / without solar panels, using cheaper off-peak electricity tariffs. That last point matters. Despite the name, home battery storage is not only for homes with solar panels. More households are now considering battery-only storage to charge from cheaper off-peak electricity and use that stored power later when rates are higher.' // Installed cost table: 'Home battery without solar / Standalone home battery / £4,000–£8,000+' and 'Small home battery: £4,000–£5,500 / Medium home battery: £5,500–£7,000 / Larger premium battery: £7,000–£8,000+' // Battery model pricing: Alpha ESS G3 (10.1 kWh): supply £2,550, installation £1,400, 10-year warranty. Solax Triple Power (5.8 kWh): supply £2,100, installation £1,400, 5-year warranty. Tesla Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh): supply £5,600, installation £1,750, 10-year warranty. // VAT note: 'Qualifying residential battery installations currently benefit from 0% VAT until 31 March 2027, before reverting to the reduced 5% rate.' // On savings: 'If you don't have solar, the savings usually come from charging the battery during cheaper off-peak periods and using that stored electricity when prices are higher. Your savings depend on things like: your tariff / your usage pattern / how much electricity you use in the evening / battery size / whether you have solar panels / whether you also charge an EV or run a heat pump.' // On payback: 'Battery payback varies widely because the savings depend heavily on usage and tariff. A battery may pay back faster if you: already export a lot of solar electricity / use a lot of electricity in the evening / can charge cheaply overnight / avoid buying electricity at expensive peak rates / choose a sensibly sized battery. A battery may take longer to pay back if: the upfront cost is high / your usage is low / your tariff savings are small / the battery is oversized / you move home before getting the full benefit.' // On worth: 'Battery storage can be well worth it if you: already have solar panels and export a lot of unused electricity / use a decent amount of power in the evening / are on a time-of-use tariff / want more control over your energy usage / like the idea of buying less electricity at peak rates.' // General caution: 'So be careful with any article that throws out one magic annual saving number as if every home works the same way. It doesn't. A realistic battery quote should be based on your actual setup, not fantasy averages.'
findings.summary: For a UK household without solar panels, a standalone home battery (5–10 kWh) typically costs £4,000–£7,000 installed (0% VAT applies until March 2027). The financial case rests entirely on time-of-use tariff arbitrage — charging cheaply off-peak and discharging during expensive peak periods. The page confirms this is a legitimate use case but stresses that savings vary significantly by tariff spread, usage pattern, and battery sizing. No specific annual saving figures or payback periods are given for battery-only (no solar) scenarios, and the page explicitly warns against generic saving estimates. For a high-daytime-usage household like the one described, the savings potential may be limited since much consumption occurs during working hours rather than peak evening periods, reducing the volume of electricity the battery can usefully displace. The page does not provide granular data on round-trip efficiency, degradation rates, or tariff-specific modelling needed for a full financial assessment.

findings.title: Battery Storage Cost Calculator UK 2025/26 | Home Battery Prices
findings.rational: The webpage discusses home battery storage costs, time-of-use tariffs, battery arbitrage savings, VAT relief, and payback periods in the UK for 2025/26, all of which are directly relevant to assessing whether a home battery is financially worthwhile without solar panels for a UK household.
findings.evidence:
Does battery storage work without solar panels? Yes. You can install a battery and charge it from the grid during cheap overnight periods using a time-of-use tariff such as Octopus Agile, Go, or British Gas Electric Driver. You then use stored electricity during expensive peak hours. Without solar, payback periods are longer (often 12–18 years depending on tariff), but battery-only setups are growing as smart tariffs become more attractive.

Time-of-Use Tariffs and Battery Arbitrage: The most compelling financial case for home battery storage in 2025/26 comes from time-of-use (TOU) tariffs. Tariffs such as Octopus Agile, Octopus Go, Intelligent Octopus, E.ON Drive, and British Gas Electric Driver offer overnight rates as low as 7–10p/kWh versus peak rates of 30–40p/kWh. A battery charged overnight at 9p and discharged at 28p saves approximately 19p per kWh. A 10kWh battery cycling daily at this spread saves roughly £694 per year (10kWh × 19p × 365). Over 10 years that is £6,940 — not far from the full installed cost of a mid-range system.

Installed costs: A home battery storage system in the UK typically costs between £5,000 and £15,000 fully installed, depending on capacity and brand. A 10kWh system averages around £8,000 installed. GivEnergy All-in-One 8.2 kWh: £6,500–£8,000 (10-year warranty); Tesla Powerwall 3 13.5 kWh: £9,500–£11,500 (10-year warranty); Sonnen Eco 10 10 kWh: £8,500–£10,500 (10-year warranty); BYD Battery-Box Premium LVS 7.7–30.7 kWh: £6,000–£18,000 (10-year warranty); Sigenergy SigenStor 10 kWh: £7,500–£9,500 (10-year warranty).

VAT: Since February 2024, all standalone battery storage installations in England, Scotland, and Wales attract 0% VAT (reduced from 20%), making a significant difference to upfront costs. A £10,000 system that would have cost £12,000 with VAT is now £10,000 — a £2,000 saving. This applies until March 2027.

Usable capacity: A 10kWh rated battery delivers approximately 9–9.5kWh usable capacity (90–95% of rated). Most major brands offer 10-year warranties with performance guarantees (typically 70–80% capacity retention after 10 years). Tesla Powerwall 3 and GivEnergy batteries are rated for around 4,000 charge cycles, equating to roughly 10–15 years of daily use.

Grants: There is no dedicated government grant specifically for standalone battery storage in 2025/26, but the 0% VAT rate effectively represents a 20% saving versus the standard rate.

Smart HEMS: Smart home energy management systems (HEMS) like GivEnergy's GivAI, Tesla's Gateway software, and Sonnen's intelligent control optimise battery charging and discharging automatically, adjusting for weather forecasts, tariff pricing, and household demand patterns without manual intervention.
findings.summary: For a UK household without solar panels, a home battery can still generate savings by charging on cheap overnight TOU tariff rates (7–10p/kWh) and discharging during peak periods (30–40p/kWh), yielding roughly 19p/kWh arbitrage. A 10 kWh battery cycling daily at this spread could save approximately £694/year, giving a theoretical 10-year saving of ~£6,940 against an installed cost of ~£8,000–£10,500 — implying a simple payback of 12–18 years without solar, which the page itself acknowledges. A ~5 kWh (e.g. GivEnergy 8.2 kWh at lower end) costs £6,500–£8,000 installed. All standalone batteries now benefit from 0% VAT in England. However, the page's arbitrage calculation assumes a full 10 kWh cycle every single day, which may not be realistic given this household's high daytime consumption and limited manual shifting ability. The page does not address the possibility of switching to a TOU tariff without a battery, nor does it provide sensitivity analysis, degradation-adjusted savings, or account for tariff uncertainty — all critical factors for this household's decision.

findings.title: Solar battery costs UK: the expert guide [2026]

While the page is primarily oriented toward solar+battery systems, it contains concrete cost figures, VAT policy details, and technical characteristics applicable to standalone battery installations.
findings.evidence: Battery size costs: '~1,800 kWh annual usage → 5kWh battery: £3,000–4,000'; '~3,400 kWh annual usage → 10kWh battery: £4,000–6,000'. These prices 'include the cost of the installation and inverter.' VAT: 'In February 2024, the government added standalone solar batteries to its list of energy-saving materials that qualify for a 0% VAT rate until the end of March 2027. After that point, the government plans to raise this rate to 5% for all solar installations. Previously, most households had to pay 20% VAT to purchase a solar battery on its own.' Lifespan: 'Lithium-ion batteries are usually more expensive but have a higher average lifespan, at 10-12 years, and very few maintenance needs.' And: 'Lithium-ion solar batteries need replacing every 10-12 years, but don't need much maintenance during their useful life.' Battery quality factors: 'Make sure you check your battery's depth of discharge (DoD), as this will tell you how much of its kWh size you're able to use without degrading the battery in the long run... A battery with 100% DoD... will usually be worth more than a model with 80% DoD.' Efficiency: 'Lithium-ion batteries are usually around 96% efficient.' Discharge rate: 'The battery's rate of discharge also affects its price. If it's high, you'll be able to use smart battery controls and the best export tariffs more effectively.' Grants: The VAT discount (0%) is 'open to everyone' until March 2027. Other grants (Warm Homes: Local Grant, ECO4) are targeted at 'the most deprived and energy-inefficient households' and 'exclude most people.' Backup power adds cost: 'Some batteries can provide backup power when the grid goes down... This work will add to your overall costs.' Lead-acid batteries 'typically last three to seven years – or less, if you don't keep up with their numerous maintenance needs' and are not recommended.
findings.summary: For a UK homeowner assessing a standalone home battery without solar panels, this page provides key cost benchmarks: a 5 kWh battery installed costs roughly £3,000–£4,000 and a 10 kWh battery £4,000–£6,000 (inclusive of inverter and installation), with 0% VAT applicable to all households until March 2027 (rising to 5% thereafter). Lithium-ion batteries have a usable lifespan of 10–12 years with minimal maintenance, meaning replacement must be factored into any 10-year financial model. Usable capacity depends on depth of discharge (commonly 80–100% of rated capacity), and round-trip efficiency is approximately 96%. Most grants are restricted to low-income or energy-inefficient households, so the typical homeowner can only rely on the VAT exemption. Backup power functionality adds further installation cost. These figures establish the capital cost baseline and key technical parameters needed to calculate payback periods and 10-year net outcomes for the battery options under assessment.

The page confirms VAT exemption applies to domestic battery installations in the UK, reducing upfront cost by up to 20%, and notes that time-of-use tariffs are a key mechanism for savings. However, as a commercial installer marketing page, its cost and payback figures should be treated cautiously and cross-checked against independent sources; notably, the payback claim appears optimistic and is not broken down with transparent assumptions, and the page does not address the standalone battery (no solar) use case in detail.

findings.title: Solar Battery Storage Costs in 2026 | Checkatrade
findings.rational: This Checkatrade page covers solar battery storage costs, battery sizing, system types, and off-peak tariff compatibility. While primarily focused on solar+battery combinations, it contains directly relevant data on battery-only installed costs, usable capacity (depth of discharge), round-trip efficiency losses, AC-coupled system characteristics, and time-of-use tariff charging — all of which are needed to assess whether a standalone home battery (without solar) is financially worthwhile for the described UK household.
findings.evidence: Battery installed costs (supply and install, lithium-ion, 6,000 cycles, 10–15 year life): 4 kWh = £4,000; 5 kWh = £5,000; 8 kWh = £7,000; 10 kWh = £8,000; 16 kWh = £12,000 (last updated March 2025). Installation labour for a 4 kWh battery alone is approximately £500. A standard 4 kW inverter costs approximately £900 and has a 12-year lifespan. Battery lifespan is stated as 10–15 years, implying possible replacement within a 10-year assessment window for lower-quality units, though the 6,000-cycle rating suggests longevity at one cycle per day. Depth of discharge (DoD) is typically 80–95%, meaning usable capacity is less than the nameplate figure — a 5 kWh battery yields roughly 4.0–4.75 kWh usable; a 10 kWh battery yields roughly 8.0–9.5 kWh usable. On round-trip efficiency: 'A round trip on an AC-coupled battery can waste up to 10% of the energy used' — AC-coupled systems require double conversion (AC→DC for storage, DC→AC for use), resulting in higher losses than DC-coupled systems. DC-coupled systems have the con of 'no benefit from low-rate electricity charging,' whereas AC-coupled systems explicitly 'can be charged using cheap off-peak electricity — allows integration with grid charging and time-of-use tariffs for additional savings.' This is the relevant configuration for a no-solar household. Off-peak tariff compatibility is confirmed: 'With schemes like Economy 7 or Octopus Go, you can charge your battery during off-peak hours at a fraction of the cost of buying during the daytime. This means you can benefit from cheaper electricity even in the winter when your PV array produces very little export electricity.' Average household electricity use is cited as approximately 10 kWh/day. The page notes that 'the timing and degree of charging must be optimised from the start to preserve the battery's life' and that without proper care 'it could quickly diminish.' Stackable systems are noted as scalable but may have 'limits on discharge rate or maximum stack size.'
findings.summary: For a no-solar household assessing a standalone battery, the key figures from this source are: installed cost of approximately £5,000 for a 5 kWh battery and £8,000 for a 10 kWh battery (March 2025 estimates from a trade directory — treat as indicative, not authoritative). Usable capacity is 80–95% of nameplate, so a 5 kWh unit delivers roughly 4.0–4.75 kWh and a 10 kWh unit delivers roughly 8.0–9.5 kWh per cycle. The AC-coupled configuration (required without solar) incurs round-trip losses of up to 10%, reducing the effective value of each stored kWh. The battery lifespan of 10–15 years at 6,000 cycles is broadly consistent with one cycle per day over the assessment period, though replacement may be needed. Critically, AC-coupled batteries are confirmed compatible with off-peak time-of-use tariffs (e.g., Octopus Go, Economy 7), which is the primary savings mechanism for a no-solar household. However, this source is a trade referral platform with commercial incentives; its cost figures should be verified against manufacturer quotes and independent sources before use in financial modelling.

findings.title: Cost to Add Battery to Existing Solar Panels UK 2026
findings.rational: This webpage discusses battery storage costs and payback in the UK context, including installed prices, VAT rules, tariff arbitrage savings, and efficiency considerations. While it focuses on retrofitting batteries to existing solar panels, it contains directly relevant data on battery installation costs, off-peak tariff spreads, round-trip efficiency, and annual savings estimates that apply to the no-solar battery scenario being assessed.
findings.evidence: Most UK homeowners retrofitting a battery to an existing solar PV system pay between £3,000 and £10,500 fully installed in 2026. A 5 kWh AC-coupled battery typically costs £3,000–£5,500, a 10 kWh battery £5,000–£8,500. Under the July–September 2026 price cap, the average electricity unit rate is 26.11p/kWh (Ofgem), while EV-style off-peak tariffs charge around 7p/kWh overnight — a gap of roughly 19p on every kWh you shift. A 10 kWh battery cycled daily through winter on a ~7p overnight rate can save in the region of £1.50 a day even with zero sunshine. Scenario table (10 kWh retrofit, ~£6,500 installed): Solar self-use only — flat tariff: £200–£350/yr, 15+ years payback; + off-peak arbitrage — charge at ~7p overnight, avoid 26.11p daytime imports: £450–£700/yr, 9–14 years payback; + smart peak export — discharge to grid at up to 32.17p in the 4–7pm window: £600–£900/yr, 7–11 years payback. Round-trip efficiency for AC-coupled is ~90% (extra 3–5% conversion loss vs DC-coupled). Most quality batteries carry 10–12 year warranties. Since 1 February 2024, battery storage installed in a home is zero-rated for VAT until 31 March 2027, saving roughly £600–£1,750 versus 20% VAT. GivEnergy entered administration in April 2026, leaving owners facing uncertainty over warranty support. A battery on a standard variable tariff leaves most of the value on the table. Nominal vs usable capacity: a '10 kWh' unit may deliver 9–9.5 kWh per cycle.
findings.summary: For a no-solar household, the most relevant data from this page is the off-peak arbitrage opportunity: with grid rates at ~26.11p/kWh and off-peak tariffs at ~7p/kWh, there is a ~19p/kWh spread. A 10 kWh battery (installed ~£5,000–£8,500, 0% VAT until March 2027) used purely for grid arbitrage could save £450–£700/year, implying a payback of roughly 9–14 years — at the edge of or beyond a 10-year assessment window. Without solar, the 'smart peak export' scenario is less applicable. AC-coupled round-trip efficiency is ~90%, usable capacity is typically 9–9.5 kWh for a nominal 10 kWh unit, and manufacturer stability (e.g. GivEnergy's 2026 administration) is a material risk. Tariff switching alone — to a ~7p off-peak rate — provides meaningful savings without any hardware cost, making it the lowest-risk first step.

findings.title: Octopus Energy tariffs July 2026 | Fixed, Tracker, Agile, Go
findings.rational: The webpage details Octopus Energy's July 2026 tariff lineup, including time-of-use tariffs (Agile, Go, Intelligent Go, Cosy, Flux) with specific unit rates and off-peak windows. This is directly relevant to comparing flat-rate vs time-of-use tariff options for a UK household considering a home battery, as the tariff spread between off-peak and peak rates is the fundamental driver of battery economics without solar.
findings.evidence: Octopus 12M Fixed v18: £1,632/yr TDCV, cap-aligned single rate, no exit fees. Ofgem cap now £1,862/yr since 1 July 2026. Octopus Tracker v3: averaging £1,488/yr mid-July 2026 (volatile, daily-priced on wholesale). Octopus Agile: averaging £1,520/yr July 2026, half-hourly day-ahead pricing; 'Bills are 10–25% lower than Fixed v18 for households that can avoid the 16:00–19:00 peak window (when prices regularly hit 50–80p/kWh). Worst for homes with cookers, dishwashers and tumble dryers running through the early evening peak. Best for homes with batteries, smart appliances, and the discipline to time-shift.' Octopus Go: 8.5p/kWh off-peak (00:30–05:30), 30.1p peak, standard standing charge. Intelligent Octopus Go: 7p/kWh off-peak (23:30–05:30, six-hour window with smart extension), standard peak rate, requires compatible EV/charger — 'The 7p rate also applies to all household electricity used during the smart-controlled window, not just car charging.' Octopus Flux: variable import/export by half-hour, export 5–29.32p/kWh, 'Best for households with a 5+ kWh home battery that can store solar generation and discharge during peak windows. Typical Flux households see net bills 30–60% lower than standard variable for the import portion, plus meaningful export earnings.' Intelligent Octopus Flux: AI-managed, peak export up to 32.17p/kWh, requires compatible battery (Tesla Powerwall 2/3, GivEnergy AIO, Fox ESS and others). 'For smart-home enthusiasts with a battery, Agile or Tracker can comfortably beat Fixed v18 — at the cost of monthly bill variability.' Smart meter requirement: 'If you're switching to Tracker, Agile or any of the smart tariffs, you'll need a SMETS2 smart meter in half-hourly settlement mode.' The household already has a smart meter. Octopus Go and Intelligent Go are classified as EV tariffs, but Intelligent Go's 7p rate applies to all household electricity in the window.
findings.summary: As of July 2026, the most relevant Octopus tariffs for a non-solar battery household are: Octopus Go (8.5p off-peak / 30.1p peak, 5-hour window) and Octopus Agile (half-hourly wholesale pricing, averaging ~£1,520/yr at TDCV, with peak prices of 50–80p/kWh during 16:00–19:00 but potentially 10–25% cheaper than Fixed v18 for load-shifting households). The flat Fixed v18 rate is cap-aligned at approximately 24–25p/kWh (implied by £1,632/yr TDCV). The key tariff spread for battery arbitrage on Octopus Go is roughly 8.5p (off-peak charge) vs 30.1p (peak discharge avoidance), a spread of ~21.6p/kWh. On Agile, the spread is wider but variable. Flux and Intelligent Flux are designed for solar+battery and are less applicable here. The household's SMETS2 smart meter satisfies the switching requirement. Critically, Intelligent Go's 7p rate applies to all household electricity in the window — not just EV charging — making it potentially the most attractive off-peak rate (7p vs 30.1p+ peak, ~23p spread) if the household can qualify without an EV, though eligibility without a compatible EV or charger is unclear from this source.

findings.title: How do I get the energy price cut from April 2026? | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: This webpage discusses Octopus Energy's April 2026 price cap changes, including unit rate reductions and standing charge adjustments. It provides context on current UK electricity pricing under the price cap, which is directly relevant to establishing the baseline flat-rate tariff cost and understanding the current electricity pricing environment for the household assessment.
findings.evidence: On a variable tariff at the max energy price cap, the savings will be equivalent to around £117 a year for a typical medium-sized house. On a fixed tariff, the savings will be equivalent to around £130 per year for a typical medium-sized house. The average dual-fuel bill drops from £1,758 down to £1,641 — an overall saving of £117. Policy costs are down £130. Wholesale costs are down £38. Other costs are down £15. Network costs are up £66. The government is removing £126 linked to green levies from your bills and they've promised to keep it that way until 2029. Overall, gas standing charges have fallen but electricity standing charges have risen slightly. Some costs (about £35) associated with delivering the Warm Home Discount scheme have been moved from the standing charge to the unit rate. The Energy Company Obligation scheme has been scrapped, slicing £60 off annual energy bills. 75% of the costs associated with the Renewables Obligation will be shifted to general taxation until 2029, reducing energy bills by £66 this year.
findings.summary: This page confirms that as of April 2026, UK electricity prices under the price cap have fallen, with the typical dual-fuel bill now around £1,641/year. It does not provide specific unit rates relevant to the household's £0.247/kWh flat rate assumption, nor does it address time-of-use tariffs, home batteries, or the financial case for battery storage. Its primary relevance is confirming the current pricing environment: electricity policy levies have been reduced and are promised stable until 2029, which slightly reduces the financial incentive for battery arbitrage by lowering the overall unit rate baseline. The page offers no data on off-peak/peak tariff spreads, battery costs, or savings calculations relevant to the battery assessment.

findings.title: Energy prices from April 2026, and what they mean for you | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: This Octopus Energy page discusses the July 2026 Ofgem price cap update, including the current maximum unit rate for electricity on variable tariffs (26.11p/kWh) and standing charges. This is directly relevant to establishing the baseline flat-rate electricity cost the household would face without a battery, and for comparing against time-of-use tariffs like Octopus Agile or Intelligent Octopus Go.
findings.evidence: From the page: 'From July 1, energy prices are rising. The Ofgem price cap will climb by 13.5% (pushing a typical, medium-sized home's bill for gas and electricity up £221 to £1,862 on average).' And: 'Ofgem have shared that on average - for customers paying by direct debit - the unit rates (inc. VAT) will be: Electric: 26.11 pence per kWh, 57.19 pence daily standing charge.' The page also notes: 'We remain the only large supplier to have never charged the full Ofgem price cap for our flexible tariff.' Additionally: 'The price cap represents the maximum amount Ofgem considers fair for energy suppliers to charge customers on variable tariffs.' And: 'If you use more - or less - energy than that typical home, your own yearly energy costs on a tariff priced at the maximum rates may be higher - or lower - than the annual figure from Ofgem.' Typical consumption figures used: 2,700 kWh electricity and 11,500 kWh gas (Octopus's retained figures), with Ofgem's revised figures being 2,500 kWh electricity and 9,500 kWh gas.
findings.summary: As of July 2026, the Ofgem price cap sets the maximum electricity unit rate at 26.11p/kWh (direct debit, average across regions) with a 57.19p/day standing charge. This is the effective ceiling for a standard variable flat-rate tariff. The household in question pays approximately 24.7p/kWh, which is already below the price cap maximum, consistent with Octopus's claim of pricing below the cap. For the financial comparison: at 9,000 kWh/year on a flat rate of ~24.7p/kWh, the annual electricity unit cost is approximately £2,223 (plus standing charges of ~£209/year, totalling ~£2,432/year). This establishes the Option 1 baseline. The cap rate of 26.11p/kWh would yield ~£2,350 in unit costs alone (~£2,559 total), confirming the household's current tariff is competitive. Any time-of-use tariff or battery strategy must be benchmarked against this ~24.7p/kWh flat rate to assess genuine savings potential.

findings.rational: This Ofgem page provides the official energy price cap unit rates and standing charges for Q3 2026, which are directly relevant to establishing the baseline electricity cost for a UK household and understanding the regulatory ceiling on flat-rate tariffs against which time-of-use tariff savings and battery economics must be compared.

The big number to remember is that VPP income is the topping, not the base. The base is tariff arbitrage on a time-of-use plan, worth roughly £800 to £950 a year on Octopus Go for the typical UK three- to four-bed home. Tax: HMRC's trading and miscellaneous income allowance lets you earn up to £1,000 a year before declaring. VPP payments fall inside this for almost every domestic battery.

findings.title: Home Battery Storage Without Solar: Save £5,200+ in 2026 | UK Guide
findings.rational: This webpage directly addresses the goal of assessing whether a home battery without solar panels is financially worthwhile in the UK, covering installed costs, tariff comparisons, payback calculations, round-trip efficiency, battery degradation, and kill criteria — all central to the research question.
findings.evidence:
From the payback worksheet section: 'Formula (estimate): daily saving ~ usable kWh x (peak – off-peak) x RTE. Payback years ~ system cost / (daily saving x cycling days per year).' Worked example: 'Usable capacity 10 kWh usable (example), Off-peak rate 7p/kWh, Peak rate 28p/kWh, Round-trip efficiency 90% RTE, Spread after losses (28 – 7) x 0.90 = 18.9p per kWh cycled, Daily saving if full cycle 10 x £0.189 = £1.89/day, Annual saving at 330 cycles £1.89 x 330 ~ £624/year. If that example system cost £2,800 all-in, simple payback is about 4.5 years.'

From the Economy Seven tariff case using a 16.1kWh Fogstar battery: 'Unit rate (day) 35.17p/kWh, Unit rate (night) 14.75p/kWh. kWh price difference 20.42p/kWh. kWh stored and used per day (80% of 16.1kWh) 12.88 kWh. Savings per day £2.63. Break-even days 1,254 (3.4 years). Savings at 6000 cycles £15,780.' System cost breakdown: 'Inverter: Sunsynk 3.6 ECCO £750, New AC breaker from a qualified electrician: £240, Battery storage: 16.1kWh Fogstar Energy £1,749.99, Total: £3,300 (rounded).'

Comparison baseline: 'Total without Economy Seven and batteries = 6000 days x 12kWh x 27.69p/kWh = £19,937. We get £19,937 – £14,700 = £5,237 benefit.'

From the Agile tariff case: 'Unit rate (higher rate) 21.4p/kWh, Unit rate (low rate) 11.5p/kWh. kWh price difference 9.9p/kWh. Savings per day £1.28. Break-even days 2,578 (7.1 years). Savings at 6000 cycles £7,680.'

Kill criteria: 'Low peak/off-peak spread: if the gap after RTE is under about 10p/kWh, daily savings rarely cover a multi-thousand-pound system in a sensible time. You will not cycle daily: a battery that sits full most of the week only earns on rare days; the worksheet needs honest cycling days, not the calendar maximum. No TOU tariff available: on a flat single unit rate, battery-only storage has almost no arbitrage income left.'

On battery degradation: 'The cycle life of the batteries used in this 2026 example is 6,000+ cycles at 1C to 80% depth of discharge. Modern LiFePO4 technology ensures that after 6,000 cycles, you will still have a battery delivering 80% of its stated capacity.'

On VAT: 'Standalone battery storage currently qualifies for zero-rated VAT. After March 2027, expect 5% VAT, adding around £150 to a £3,000 system.'

On tariff uncertainty and financial risks: 'Energy prices can fluctuate, affecting your savings. Batteries degrade over time, reducing their storage capacity.'

On daily cycling assumption: 'a battery that sits full most of the week only earns on rare days; the worksheet needs honest cycling days, not the calendar maximum' and 'Days per year you actually cycle the pack' is listed as a required input, explicitly warning against assuming 365 cycles.

On the high-daytime-consumption profile relevance: The page notes the household example uses 12kWh/day as a 'typical high consumption case' and that the battery covers all daily consumption in the Economy Seven scenario, but this implicitly assumes the battery can discharge during daytime peak hours — relevant to a home-office user with high daytime demand who needs the battery to discharge during the day rather than evening.
findings.summary: The webpage provides a directly relevant, worked financial analysis of home battery storage without solar in the UK as of July 2026. Key findings: a ~16kWh battery system costs approximately £3,300 all-in (DIY-assisted); on Octopus Economy Seven (14.75p off-peak / 35.17p peak), payback is ~3.4 years with ~£5,237 net benefit over 6,000 cycles versus a flat 27.69p/kWh tariff. On Octopus Agile (11.5p low / 21.4p high), the spread is narrower, pushing payback to ~7.1 years. The core formula is: daily saving = usable kWh × (peak − off-peak) × RTE, with RTE typically 85–92% for LiFePO4. The page explicitly warns against assuming daily full cycles and lists thin spreads (<~10p/kWh after losses), infrequent cycling, and absence of a TOU tariff as project kill criteria. LiFePO4 batteries retain 80% capacity after 6,000 cycles. 0% VAT applies until March 2027. The page does not provide a standalone 'tariff switch without battery' savings figure, nor does it model a 5 kWh battery specifically, and its cycling assumptions (near-daily full cycles on 12kWh/day consumption) may be optimistic for a 9,000 kWh/year household with high fixed daytime demand that cannot easily be shifted to off-peak hours.

findings.title: How cheap is battery storage? | Ember
findings.rational: This webpage from Ember discusses utility-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) costs, LCOS, efficiency, degradation, and lifetime assumptions. While focused on large commercial/grid-scale systems rather than residential home batteries in the UK, it provides relevant benchmark data on battery economics including round-trip efficiency, degradation rates, operational costs, and levelised cost of storage that can inform the residential assessment — particularly as reference points for comparing manufacturer claims against real-world performance data.
findings.evidence: All-in BESS project capex of $125/kWh for utility-scale long-duration (4+ hour) systems outside China and the US as of October 2025, comprising ~$75/kWh for core equipment and ~$50/kWh for installation and grid connection. LFP battery cell prices have dropped to ~$40/kWh in Chinese domestic markets as of November 2025. Round-trip AC-to-AC efficiency of 90% is described as 'upper end of performance offered by leading suppliers' for 2025 installations, with older generation batteries closer to 80–85%. Annual degradation is typically guaranteed at ≤2% per year by manufacturers, meaning after 20 years capacity remains at ~65% of initial usable energy. A 20-year design lifetime is now standard for LFP technology, with performance guarantees of 10,000–12,000+ cycles. Annual operational costs for battery storage are typically ~2% of capex. The LCOS of $65/MWh is based on: 20-year lifetime, 7% discount rate, 90% round-trip efficiency, 80% utilisation (less than one full cycle per day), 2% annual degradation, and 2% annual operational costs. Notably, 'long duration systems (4 hours or more) can rarely achieve more than one full cycle per day' and the 80% utilisation figure is described as a conservative estimate for solar-shifting applications. Smaller projects 'may not get such competitive quotes from Chinese manufacturers' and costs can be 10–15% higher for shorter-duration (sub-4-hour) systems because some components are sized to power (MW) rather than energy (MWh).
findings.summary: This Ember report on utility-scale BESS costs provides useful technical benchmarks for the residential battery assessment, though it must be applied cautiously given the vast scale difference. Key transferable insights are: (1) Round-trip efficiency of 90% represents best-in-class for 2025 LFP systems; residential units are likely 85–90% AC-to-AC. (2) Degradation of ~2%/year is a manufacturer-guaranteed ceiling, meaning a 5–10 kWh residential battery will lose meaningful capacity over a 10-year horizon (roughly 18–20% capacity loss by year 10). (3) Fewer than one full cycle per day is realistic even for optimised systems — directly supporting the instruction not to assume a full daily cycle for the home battery. (4) Annual operational/maintenance costs of ~2% of capex are a reasonable baseline. (5) Utility-scale installed costs of $125/kWh are far below residential installed costs (typically £800–£1,200/kWh in the UK), confirming that residential battery economics are substantially less favourable than grid-scale economics. These figures should be used as technical reference points rather than cost benchmarks for the UK home battery comparison.
